one_liner: C++ rewrite of Apache Cassandra (CQL, plus a DynamoDB API) on a thread-per-core engine; vendor claims 3-8x Cassandra 4.0 throughput.
what_it_does: A distributed wide-column NoSQL database that speaks Cassandra's CQL (protocol v4 with some v5 features) and reads Cassandra 3.11/2.x SSTable formats, with Amazon DynamoDB's API available as the optional Alternator interface. Its own docs call it a drop-in replacement for Cassandra 3.11 with some 4.0 features: existing drivers, schemas and cqlsh workflows carry over, but it is a server you deploy, not a library you link.
how_it_is_fast: Built on the Seastar framework: one pinned thread per core (shard-per-core, shared-nothing), futures-based asynchronous code with no locks between cores, and every partition owned by exactly one shard; shard-aware drivers can connect straight to the owning shard via the SCYLLA_SHARD_AWARE_PORT protocol extension. It claims all RAM at start-up and keeps its own row cache (row-granular LRU eviction) and memtables in a log-structured allocator (LSA, 128 KiB segments with memory compaction) instead of relying on the OS page cache and a JVM heap, so there are no GC pauses. Seastar CPU and I/O schedulers with share-based scheduling groups and a backlog-driven compaction controller keep compaction, streaming and repair from starving foreground queries.
when_to_use: You run Cassandra (CQL) or DynamoDB-style key-value/wide-column workloads and want higher throughput per node or fewer nodes at a P99 latency target.
Dedicated Linux machines or large cloud instances with local NVMe (the vendor tests used AWS i3.4xlarge and i3.metal) where the database may own every core and nearly all memory.
Read-heavy workloads whose hot set fits in the row cache, or write-heavy time-series data with TWCS/ICS compaction.
Small deployments that stay within the source-available licence's caps (10 TB total storage, 50 vCPUs) and are not run as a SaaS/DBaaS, or teams prepared to buy a commercial licence.
when_not_to_use: Analytical scans, joins or ad hoc SQL: it is an OLTP wide-column store with lightweight transactions only, despite this catalog's columnar-analytics category; pick a column-store engine instead.

You need an open-source (OSI) licence, a large self-hosted cluster, or a managed offering of your own: the ScyllaDB Software License Agreement v1.1 limits use to 'Never Customers', caps storage at 10 TB and 50 vCPUs, bans SaaS/DBaaS and competing use, and assigns your modifications to the licensor.

Cassandra features it lacks: Triggers, SAI (except for vector search), Incremental Repair, super columns, Thrift (dropped in 6.0), dynamic snitching and non-Murmur3 partitioners; User Defined Functions are marked unavailable for Cassandra compatibility and only experimental.
Shared or overcommitted hosts (laptops, busy Kubernetes nodes): by default it pins threads and claims all memory; --smp/--memory/--overprovisioned reduce that, at a performance cost.

Clusters with frequent topology changes under tight P99 budgets: open issues report P99 spikes during node add/decommission, tablet split/merge, repair and compaction (e.g. #20895, #23441, #24025, #3615).

integration.dependencies: Server binary; built from source with Seastar (git submodule), Ninja and a recent C++23 toolchain, ideally via the frozen 'dbuild' Docker/Podman toolchain; clients use any CQL or DynamoDB driver (shard-aware drivers recommended).
integration.min_toolchain: C++23 compiler (HACKING.md also says GCC >= 10, an older note; the frozen toolchain is the supported path); about 2 GB RAM per build thread, 3 GB when linking.
integration.platforms: 64-bit Linux only; x86-64 with SSE4.2 required (will not boot without it) and AArch64 including AWS Graviton.
integration.thread_safety: N/A as a server; internally one thread per core with data partitioned by shard; clients connect concurrently over CQL.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — the project documents itself as a drop-in replacement for Cassandra 3.11 (CQL and SSTable compatible), but some Cassandra features (Triggers, SAI, Incremental Repair, Cassandra-compatible UDFs) are missing, and configuration and operations tooling differ.

gotchas: The performance claims are vendor-run (2021, ScyllaDB 4.4.3 vs Cassandra 4.0) with no public harness; the '4 vs 40' test pits 4 i3.metal nodes (288 vCPUs) on CentOS 7.9 against 40 i3.4xlarge nodes (640 vCPUs, about 2.2x, derived from page data) on Ubuntu 20.04, and the vendor concedes Cassandra has lower latency at low throughput there.
Today's licence is not the one the benchmarked 'Scylla Open Source 4.4' shipped under; the current repository is source-available only, so you cannot copy code from it into your project.
Startup checks expect a tuned machine; --developer-mode 1 disables them, and the setup scripts tune IRQs and disks, so untuned installs can underperform the published numbers.
Compaction needs headroom: the docs recommend keeping 50% (LCS/TWCS) to 70% (ICS) disk utilisation at most, and a 30:1 disk-to-RAM ratio (100:1 maximum).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over YugabyteDB when you need Cassandra/DynamoDB-API throughput rather than SQL and distributed ACID transactions, and over TDengine or QuestDB when the data is general wide-column key-value rather than time series; for analytics use a sibling such as Apache Doris, StarRocks or DuckDB-class engines instead.
verified_claims_summary: ScyllaDB's own 2021 cassandra-stress tests (ScyllaDB 4.4.3 vs Apache Cassandra 4.0 on equal 3-node AWS i3.4xlarge clusters) report 3x-8x Cassandra's throughput at P99 under 10 ms (white-paper table 2.66x-8x), and in a 4 i3.metal vs 40 i3.4xlarge test, comparable or higher throughput plus 11x faster node addition and 32x faster major compaction; all vendor-run, seen only through search-result text, with no compiler, CPU-model or harness published and no independent replication found (a 2025 Applied Computer Systems YCSB study's abstract favours ScyllaDB on several features but its numbers were not seen).
status_note: Very actively developed (commits through 2026-10-23, 15.8k stars), but the current source-available licence (v1.1, April 2026) makes it a reference implementation rather than copyable code, and free use is capped at 10 TB and 50 vCPUs for non-customers.
